source.title: C3P: Contrastive promoter-protein pretraining yields representations capturing bacterial gene regulation
source.authors: Cameron Dufault; Scott Xu; Alan M. Moses

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures downstream-task performance across model scales, a different outcome from held-out language-model cross-entropy, and reports how performance changes with scale.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out cross-entropy or fit loss power laws. Its relevant results are downstream regulatory-function evaluations across C3P sizes and a promoter-activity evaluation. The gLM comparisons in the scaling figures are not separately itemized here; the text describes their gains with scale as minor.
record.test_reason: The study measures downstream task performance across four C3P sizes (1M–100M trainable parameters, ~1e19–1.7e20 FLOPS) and plots it against pretraining compute, along with gLM families. This is a new setting for V6: a contrastive promoter-protein encoder in bacterial genomics, not an autoregressive text LM. The result is a qualitative scale trend with no fitted law and no loss measurement. The link to V6 is therefore loose: the system is not a language model, and only four points are given, in figures. V1–V5 and V7 are not tested. The 6ND FLOPS heuristic is borrowed from Kaplan et al. only as a tool.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that C3P scales favourably relative to gLMs on regulatory inference, with gLM gains from scale minor and costly. They caveat that C3P uses a pretrained frozen protein encoder while the gLMs were trained from scratch, and that only trainable parameter size was varied. The promoter-activity result (1M/5M best) is reported in Appendix H but is not framed by the authors as a scaling conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: This is contrastive promoter-protein pretraining and downstream regulatory evaluation, not autoregressive language-model pretraining evaluated by held-out cross-entropy. C3P's protein encoder is frozen and pretrained.
record.method_sensitivity: The result depends on the downstream task: C3P scales favorably on regulatory classification and retrieval, while the 1M and 5M variants perform best on promoter-activity prediction.
record.problems: The scaling results are shown in figures without numerical values stated in text; only four C3P sizes are tested. The study evaluates downstream biological tasks rather than held-out loss, and the authors note that C3P uses a pretrained protein encoder whereas comparison gLMs were trained from scratch.
record.rows_left_out: Individual gLM points in Figures 6 and 8 and non-C3P model points in Figure 9 are not separately itemized; the text reports only that gLM scaling gains are minor and that the best-performing gLM varies by promoter-activity dataset.

untested.parts: No held-out loss is measured or fitted versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No fit on small runs and no extrapolation.
Shape is varied jointly with size (layers, heads, width), never at a fixed parameter count.
No power-law form is fitted in this genomic contrastive regime; only a qualitative downstream trend is reported.
No fitted predictive law, no relation to pretraining loss, and no extrapolation. Only four sizes; data and epochs are held fixed while trainable parameters vary.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: Numeric 100M values from Tables 1–2 (regulon 1-nn precision 0.212; full/any-match 0.242/0.402) should be attached to r4, r8 and r12.

gLM family scaling (PromoGen2 8M/33M/149M, gLM2 150M/650M, Evo vs Evo2) on the same downstream tasks, which the text says shows only minor gains with scale. This is the only language-model downstream-scaling evidence in the paper. It is declared in rows_left_out, but a researcher comparing V6 studies would need it.

record.verdict_notes: The fit to the claim is weak. C3P is a CLIP-style contrastive promoter encoder, not a language model; the scaling evidence is four figure-only points with no fitted law; and data and epochs are held fixed. The rows stand because they measure downstream performance versus scale, the measure V6 names, but readers should weigh the system mismatch. Rows r1, r5, r9, r13, r17 and r21 (the 1M models) are reference points, not effects. The reversed states for the promoter-activity rows rest on the text's statement that 1M/5M are best, not on read values.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
No loss-law fits or extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No test of whether power-law loss scaling transfers across modalities or training regimes.
The study tests downstream-task performance across model sizes and compute, but not downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss, or a fitted predictive law.
No comparison of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits under alternative fitting or setup choices.
